module_title: Asian Street Food: Noodles and Rice

lessons.title: Wok Skills and Seasoning
lessons.body:
A wok is your most important tool for Asian street food. If you don't have one, a large frying pan or karahi works, but a carbon steel wok is best. Season it before first use: scrub off the factory coating, dry it, then heat it over high heat until it turns blue. Rub with oil and heat again until smoking. Repeat three times. After each use, wash with hot water and a soft brushâno soapâthen dry and rub with a thin layer of oil. This builds a non-stick surface.

High heat is key. Street food woks are cooked over roaring flames. At home, use the highest heat your stove can give. Let the wok heat until a drop of water evaporates instantly. Add oil (groundnut or sunflower) around the rim so it coats the sides. Cook in small batchesânever overcrowd. For a family-sized portion, 200g of noodles or rice at a time is ideal. Stir constantly with a metal spatula, tossing food from the bottom to the sides.

Seasoning is not just salt. The core trio is soy sauce, fish sauce, and sugar. For every 2 tablespoons of soy sauce, add 1 teaspoon of fish sauce and 1 teaspoon of sugar. This balances salty, umami, and sweet. For heat, add chili flakes or fresh chilies. For acidity, lime juice or tamarind. Always taste after seasoningâremember that soy sauce reduces and concentrates as it cooks.

Common mistakes: adding cold food to a cold wok (it steams instead of fries), stirring too slowly (food burns), and adding sauce too early (it burns). Add sauces at the end, toss for 30 seconds, and serve immediately. In Africa, you can find woks in large markets or online. A 14-inch flat-bottom wok fits most home stoves. With practice, you'll get the 'wok hei'âthe smoky flavor that defines great street food.

lessons.title: Classic Noodle Dishes: Pad Thai, Chow Mein, and Ramen
lessons.body:
Pad Thai is Thailand's most famous noodle dish. Soak 200g of flat rice noodles in warm water for 20 minutes until flexible but not soft. Make the sauce: 2 tbsp tamarind paste, 2 tbsp fish sauce, 1 tbsp palm sugar (or brown sugar), 1 tsp chili flakes. Stir until sugar dissolves. Heat your wok, add 2 tbsp oil, then 100g sliced chicken or tofu. Cook until golden. Push aside, crack in 1 egg, scramble. Add 100g prawns, cook 1 minute. Add drained noodles and sauce. Toss for 2 minutes. Add 100g bean sprouts and 2 spring onions, toss 30 seconds. Serve with crushed peanuts, lime wedge, and extra chili.

Chow Mein is the Chinese stir-fried noodle. Use 200g egg noodles, boiled until just tender, then drained and tossed with 1 tsp sesame oil to prevent sticking. Heat wok, add oil, then 100g sliced beef or chicken. Stir-fry until browned. Add 1 sliced onion, 2 sliced carrots, 100g shredded cabbage. Cook 2 minutes. Add noodles, 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp oyster sauce, 1 tsp sugar. Toss for 2 minutes. Add 2 chopped spring onions. Serve hot.

Ramen is a Japanese noodle soup. For quick broth: boil 1 litre water with 2 tbsp miso paste, 1 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tsp sesame oil, 1 clove grated garlic, 1 tsp grated ginger. Simmer 5 minutes. Cook 200g ramen noodles separately (fresh or dried) until tender. Drain. Place noodles in bowls, pour hot broth over. Top with sliced boiled egg, corn, spinach, and sliced pork or chicken. In Africa, you can use local ingredients: replace miso with groundnut paste for a rich, nutty broth. Add chili for heat. Always cook noodles separately to avoid cloudy broth.

For all three dishes, prep everything before you turn on the heat. Chop vegetables, measure sauces, and have noodles ready. Cooking takes minutes, so no time to chop later. Use a large wok or pan. Serve immediatelyânoodles get soggy if left standing. For takeaway, pack sauce separately if possible, or toss just before serving.

lessons.title: Fried Rice Variations: Yangzhou, Kimchi, and Pineapple
lessons.body:
Fried rice is the ultimate street foodâcheap, fast, and adaptable. The golden rule: use cold, day-old rice. Fresh rice is too wet and will steam instead of fry. Spread cooked rice on a tray and refrigerate uncovered for at least 2 hours, or overnight. Break up any clumps with wet hands. For each portion, use 200g cooked rice.

Yangzhou fried rice is the classic Chinese version. Heat wok, add 2 tbsp oil. Scramble 1 egg, remove. Add 100g diced chicken, 50g diced prawns, 50g diced ham or sausage. Stir-fry 2 minutes. Add 50g peas, 50g diced carrots, 2 chopped spring onions. Cook 1 minute. Add rice, 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tsp sesame oil, 1 tsp salt. Toss for 3 minutes until heated through. Return egg, mix. Serve.

Kimchi fried rice is Korean and spicy. Heat wok, add 1 tbsp oil. Add 100g chopped kimchi and 1 tbsp kimchi juice. Stir-fry 1 minute. Add 100g diced pork or spam. Cook 2 minutes. Add 200g cold rice, 1 tbsp gochujang (or chili paste), 1 tsp soy sauce, 1 tsp sugar. Toss for 3 minutes. Top with a fried egg and chopped spring onions. For a local twist, use fermented vegetables like ugba or iru for umami.

Pineapple fried rice is Thai-inspired. Heat wok, add oil. Stir-fry 100g chicken or tofu with 1 tbsp curry powder for 1 minute. Add 50g raisins, 50g cashews, 100g diced pineapple, 2 chopped spring onions. Cook 1 minute. Add rice, 2 tbsp fish sauce, 1 tsp sugar, 1 tsp soy sauce. Toss 3 minutes. Serve in a hollowed pineapple half for presentation.

Key tips: high heat, small batches, and don't stir too muchâlet the rice sit for 30 seconds between tosses to get crispy bits. Add sauces at the end. For takeaway, pack in a paper box or foil container. Fried rice reheats well, but best fresh. In Africa, use local rice like jollof or basmatiâboth work. Adjust seasoning to taste.

lessons.title: Dumplings and Bao: Steaming and Frying
lessons.body:
Dumplings (jiaozi) and bao (steamed buns) are popular street snacks. Start with dumpling wrappers: mix 300g plain flour with 150ml warm water. Knead 10 minutes until smooth. Rest 30 minutes. Roll into a log, cut into 20 pieces, roll each into a thin circle (about 8cm wide). For filling: 300g minced pork or chicken, 100g chopped cabbage, 2 spring onions, 1 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tsp grated ginger, 1 tsp sesame oil, 1 tsp salt. Mix well.

To fold: place 1 tbsp filling in center. Moisten edges with water. Fold in half, pleat one side. Press to seal. For beginners, simply press edges with a fork. Steam: line a steamer with cabbage leaves or baking paper. Arrange dumplings without touching. Steam over boiling water for 10 minutes. For fried (potstickers): heat 2 tbsp oil in a pan, add dumplings flat side down, fry 2 minutes. Add 100ml water, cover, steam 6 minutes. Uncover, cook until water evaporates and bottoms are crispy.

Bao buns are softer. Dough: 300g flour, 1 tsp yeast, 1 tsp sugar, 150ml warm water, 1 tbsp oil. Knead, rest 1 hour until doubled. Punch down, divide into 10 balls. Flatten each, add 1 tbsp filling (same as dumplings or BBQ pork). Pleat and seal. Steam 15 minutes. For quick bao, use ready-made wrappers from Asian shops.

For takeaway, steam dumplings and pack in paper boxes with a small container of dipping sauce: 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp vinegar, 1 tsp chili oil, 1 tsp sugar. In Africa, you can use local ingredients: replace cabbage with spinach or kale, pork with beef or goat. Serve with sweet chili sauce or groundnut sauce. Dumplings freeze wellâfreeze on a tray, then bag. Cook from frozen, adding 2 minutes to steaming time.

lessons.title: Sauces and Condiments: Soy, Chili Oil, and Hoisin
lessons.body:
Sauces make or break Asian street food. Learn to make three core condiments: soy sauce blend, chili oil, and hoisin. Soy sauce blend: mix 100ml light soy sauce, 50ml dark soy sauce, 1 tbsp sugar, 1 tsp sesame oil, 1 clove grated garlic. Simmer 1 minute. Cool. This keeps for 2 weeks in the fridge. Use for dipping, stir-fries, and noodles.

Chili oil is essential. Heat 200ml groundnut oil to smoking. Meanwhile, in a heatproof bowl, combine 3 tbsp chili flakes, 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp sugar, 2 sliced garlic cloves, 1 tbsp sesame seeds. Pour hot oil over, stir. Let cool. Store in a jarâkeeps for months. For extra flavor, add 1 star anise and 1 bay leaf to the oil while heating, then remove. In Africa, use local chilies like bird's eye or scotch bonnet. Adjust heat to taste.

Hoisin sauce is sweet and tangy. Mix 4 tbsp soy sauce, 2 tbsp peanut butter (or groundnut paste), 1 tbsp honey, 1 tbsp vinegar, 1 tsp garlic powder, 1 tsp chili paste. Simmer 2 minutes. Use for dipping, glazing, or stir-fries. For a quick version, buy ready-made hoisin and thin with water.

Other condiments: sweet chili sauce (mix 4 tbsp sugar, 2 tbsp water, 2 tbsp vinegar, 1 tbsp chili flakes, 1 tsp cornflourâsimmer until thick). Peanut sauce: 4 tbsp groundnut paste, 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp lime juice, 1 tsp sugar, 1 clove garlic, 50ml waterâblend. Serve with satay or noodles.

For takeaway, pack sauces in small sealed containers. Label if spicy. Always offer extra chili oil and soy sauce on the side. In Africa, you can make soy sauce from scratch by fermenting soybeans, but it's time-consumingâbuy from Asian shops or supermarkets. Store all sauces in clean jars, refrigerated. Taste before serving; adjust salt, sugar, or heat.

lessons.title: Packaging and Serving Noodles for Take Away
lessons.body:
Takeaway packaging must keep noodles hot, prevent sogginess, and be easy to carry. For noodles, use paper boxes with a lining or foil containers. Avoid thin plasticâit leaks and doesn't insulate. For soups like ramen, use sturdy plastic or paper bowls with tight lids. Pack broth separately if possible: give noodles and toppings in one container, hot broth in a flask or sealed jar. Customer pours broth over noodles at home. This prevents noodles from turning mushy.

For stir-fried noodles (pad thai, chow mein), pack in a paper box. Add a piece of baking paper between noodles and lid to absorb steam. Include a small container of sauce or lime wedge on the side. For fried rice, foil containers work wellâthey can be reheated in the oven. For dumplings, use paper boxes with a vent to prevent sweating. Always include a napkin and wooden chopsticks or a fork.

Serving temperature is critical. Keep hot food above 60Â°C. Use an insulated bag for delivery. If selling from a stall, have a hot box or cooler with hot water bottles. For cold items like summer rolls, use a separate bag. Label containers with dish name and spice level. In Africa, you can source affordable packaging from local suppliers: paper boxes, foil trays, and plastic containers are available in markets. Consider eco-friendly options like banana leaves for wrappingâthey are traditional and biodegradable.

Portion sizes: for a main dish, 300-400g total weight. For a side, 150-200g. Price accordingly. Include a small packet of soy sauce, chili oil, and chopsticks. For delivery, stack boxes carefully to avoid crushing. Use a cardboard carrier for multiple boxes. Always seal with a sticker or tape. Test your packaging: pack a hot dish, wait 20 minutes, then check if it's still hot and not soggy. Adjust as needed. Good packaging means repeat customers.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Packaging, Costing and Serving Asian Noodles & Rice for Take Away in Africa

This practical reference supports the module Asian Street Food: Noodles and Rice within the Street Food / Take Away course. It is written for African food entrepreneurs â from Nairobi's CBD to Lagos's Yaba, from Accra's Osu to Kampala's Wandegeya â who want to add high-margin Asian noodle and rice dishes to their take-away menu without importing every single input. The focus is on packaging, food safety, costing, and service logistics in tropical conditions, where heat, humidity, and transport delays can destroy a good dish before it reaches the customer.

Asian noodle and rice dishes travel well if you respect three rules: separate wet from dry, control steam, and keep hot food hot above 60Â°C. Get these right and you can sell Pad Thai, Chow Mein, Yangzhou fried rice, and steamed bao at a premium price point in any African city.

1. Packaging That Survives African Transport Realities

Most African take-away customers travel by boda-boda, matatu, okada, or on foot. Packaging must survive potholes, dust, and 30â45 minutes of transport. The two-compartment container shown above is the workhorse: noodles or rice in the larger side, protein and vegetables in the smaller side, sauce in a sealed 30â50 ml cup. This prevents the classic failure mode where Pad Thai turns into a soggy lump before the customer opens it.

For steamed bao and dumplings, use a vented paper or sugarcane-pulp clamshell. Plastic traps condensation, and condensation makes bao skin gluey. A 1 cm vent or a few punched holes allows steam to escape while keeping the bun warm. For soups like ramen or laksa, use a double-cup system: a 500 ml paper or PP bowl with a leak-proof lid, placed inside a second cup or a kraft sleeve. This gives insulation and catches spills.

Locally sourced options matter for margin. In Kenya, sugarcane bagasse clamshells from Nairobi-based suppliers cost roughly KES 12â18 per unit; in Nigeria, kraft paper bowls from Lagos converters run â¦80â150. Imported foam or PP containers can be cheaper per unit but attract environmental levies and customer criticism. Many African cities â including Rwanda nationwide and parts of Kenya â have banned single-use plastic carrier bags and some foam products, so verify local rules before ordering stock.

2. Costing a Take-Away Bowl: Real Numbers

The table below models a single 450 g chicken Chow Mein bowl sold in Nairobi, with local ingredient prices as of 2024. Your numbers will differ by city and season, but the structure is what matters.

Table 1: Unit cost model â Chicken Chow Mein take-away bowl (450 g), Nairobi, 2024
InputQuantityCost (KES)Notes
Egg noodles (dry)120 g28Local wheat noodles, not imported
Chicken thigh90 g55Bone-in, deboned in-house
Cabbage, carrot, onion100 g15Local market, morning purchase
Oil, soy, garlic, gingerâ18Bulk purchase
Packaging (container + lid + sauce cup)1 set22Bagasse + PP lid
Napkin, chopsticks/folk, branded sticker1 set8Brand building
LPG / charcoal for wokâ12High-heat wok burner
Total food + packaging cost158
Suggested selling price450~65% gross margin
Gross profit per bowl292Before rent, labour, delivery

Source: Author's cost model, benchmarked against Kenya National Bureau of Statistics Consumer Price Indices (2024) and Nairobi wholesale market prices. Verify locally before pricing.

3. Food Safety in Tropical Heat

Ambient temperatures in Lagos, Mombasa, or Dar es Salaam often exceed 30Â°C, which is squarely in the bacterial danger zone (5Â°Câ60Â°C). Cooked rice is a particular risk: Bacillus cereus spores survive cooking and multiply rapidly in warm, moist rice. Fried rice must be made from rice that was cooked and cooled quickly â ideally within 1 hour â and then reheated to above 75Â°C in the wok. Never leave cooked rice at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

â  SAFETY WARNING â COOKED RICE AND REHEATED NOODLES

Cooked rice and noodles left between 5Â°C and 60Â°C for more than 2 hours can grow Bacillus cereus and other pathogens that reheating does NOT destroy. In tropical heat this window shrinks to 1 hour. Rules: (1) Cool cooked rice within 1 hour, refrigerate below 5Â°C, and use within 24 hours. (2) Reheat only once, to above 75Â°C, in a hot wok. (3) Never mix old rice with new rice. (4) Discard any rice or noodle batch that has been out of temperature control for over 2 hours â the cost of one bowl is nothing compared to a food-poisoning incident that closes your business.

For dumplings and bao, the danger is different: raw pork or chicken filling must be steamed to a core temperature of 75Â°C. Use a probe thermometer on the first batch of every service. Steamed bao held in a warmer above 60Â°C can be sold for up to 2 hours; after that, discard or chill rapidly for the next day's frying.

4. Menu Engineering: Which Dishes Travel Best?

Not every Asian dish is a good take-away candidate. Ramen with soft-boiled egg and broth is beautiful in a restaurant but risky on a boda-boda. Use the table below to decide what to put on your delivery menu versus your dine-in menu.

Table 2: Take-away suitability and holding time for common Asian street dishes
DishTake-away suitabilityMax hold (hot, >60Â°C)Packaging note
Chow Mein / stir-fried noodlesExcellent2 hours2-compartment, sauce separate
Pad ThaiGood1.5 hoursSauce and peanuts separate; lime wedge in small cup
Yangzhou fried riceExcellent2 hoursVent lid to release steam; rice must be cooled fast
Kimchi fried riceGood1.5 hoursKimchi separate to avoid sogginess
Pineapple fried riceGood1.5 hoursPineapple releases water; drain before packing
Ramen / noodle soupFair (dine-in preferred)1 hourBroth and noodles in separate containers; assemble at destination
Steamed baoExcellent2 hoursVented paper clamshell; never sealed plastic
Fried dumplings (gyoza)Good1.5 hoursVent holes; sauce cup separate

Source: Holding times adapted from FAO/WHO Five Keys to Safer Food Manual (2006) and US FDA Food Code hot-holding guidance (2022), applied to typical African ambient conditions.

5. Sauces and Condiments: The Margin Multiplier

Soy sauce, chili oil, and hoisin are where you can differentiate and add margin. A 50 ml branded chili oil cup can sell for KES 50â80 on its own, or be bundled as a "signature sauce" that justifies a KES 100 premium on the bowl. Make your own chili oil from local dried chilies (Nigerian tatashe, Kenyan bird's eye, Ghanaian kpakpo shito) infused in sunflower oil with garlic and star anise. Hoisin can be approximated with local soy, molasses, vinegar, and five-spice. This reduces import dependency and creates a story customers will pay for.

Always pack sauces separately. Soy sauce leaking into fried rice turns it into a dark, salty mush. Use small screw-cap PP cups or heat-sealed sachets. Label with your brand sticker â this is free advertising every time the customer opens the bag.

6. Quick Reference Checklist

  • Cool rice within 1 hour of cooking; refrigerate below 5Â°C; use within 24 hours.
  • Reheat only once, in a hot wok, to above 75Â°C core temperature.
  • Pack sauce separately in sealed 30â50 ml cups to prevent sogginess.
  • Vent steamed bao and dumpling containers so condensation does not ruin the skin.
  • Hold hot food above 60Â°C and deliver within 2 hours maximum; 1 hour in peak tropical heat.
  • Verify local packaging bans (foam, single-use plastic) before ordering stock.
  • Cost every bowl including packaging, fuel, and a branded sticker â aim for 60â70% gross margin.
  • Use a probe thermometer on the first batch of every service, especially for pork and chicken dumplings.

7. Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • WHO â Five Keys to Safer Food Manual (2006): core food safety principles for street food and take-away.
  • FAO â Street Food in Urban Africa: A Review (2012): context on vending, hygiene, and consumer behaviour.
  • US FDA â Food Code 2022: hot-holding, cooling, and reheating standards used by regulators worldwide.
  • FAO â Food Loss and Waste in Africa (2020): useful for costing and waste reduction in take-away operations.
  • UNEP â Africa Waste Management Outlook (2018): packaging regulations and sustainable alternatives across African cities.

Practical Reference â Rise AFRICA Skills, Street Food / Take Away. Prices and regulations change; always verify locally before committing to stock or pricing.

quiz.q: What is the best way to season a new carbon steel wok?
options: A) Wash with soap and water
B) Heat until blue, rub with oil, and repeat three times
quiz.explanation: Heating the wok until blue and applying oil creates a non-stick patina.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid overcrowding the wok when stir-frying?
options: A) It makes the food too salty
B) It causes the food to steam instead of fry
D) It makes the wok dirty
quiz.explanation: Overcrowding lowers the temperature, so food steams rather than fries.

quiz.q: What is the core trio of seasonings for Asian stir-fries?
options: B) Soy sauce, fish sauce, and sugar
quiz.explanation: Soy sauce, fish sauce, and sugar balance salty, umami, and sweet flavors.

quiz.q: When should you add sauces to a stir-fry?
quiz.explanation: Adding sauces at the end prevents burning and preserves flavor.

quiz.q: What is 'wok hei'?
options: B) The smoky flavor from high-heat cooking
quiz.explanation: Wok hei is the complex smoky flavor achieved by cooking in a very hot wok.

quiz.q: For Pad Thai, how long should you soak flat rice noodles?
quiz.explanation: Soaking for 20 minutes makes noodles flexible but not soft.

quiz.q: Which ingredient is NOT part of traditional Pad Thai sauce?
quiz.explanation: Pad Thai sauce uses tamarind, fish sauce, and palm sugar, not soy sauce.

quiz.q: What should you toss cooked egg noodles with to prevent sticking?
quiz.explanation: A little sesame oil coats the noodles and stops them from sticking.

quiz.q: For quick ramen broth, which ingredient gives umami?
quiz.explanation: Miso paste is fermented and rich in umami flavor.

quiz.q: Why should ramen noodles be cooked separately from the broth?
options: B) To keep the broth clear
quiz.explanation: Cooking noodles separately prevents starch from clouding the broth.

quiz.q: What is the golden rule for making fried rice?
quiz.explanation: Cold day-old rice is dry and fries well without becoming mushy.

quiz.q: Which ingredient is typical in Yangzhou fried rice?
quiz.explanation: Yangzhou fried rice includes diced ham, chicken, prawns, and vegetables.

quiz.q: What gives kimchi fried rice its spicy flavor?
quiz.explanation: Gochujang is a Korean chili paste that adds heat and depth.

quiz.q: In pineapple fried rice, what is a common garnish?
quiz.explanation: Cashews add crunch and are often sprinkled on pineapple fried rice.

quiz.q: What should you do if your fried rice is too wet?
options: B) Cook longer on high heat
quiz.explanation: High heat evaporates excess moisture and crisps the rice.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between dumplings and bao?
options: A) Dumplings are fried, bao are steamed
B) Dumplings have thinner wrappers, bao are fluffy buns
C) Dumplings are sweet, bao are savory
D) Dumplings are Japanese, bao are Chinese
quiz.explanation: Dumplings use thin wrappers, while bao are made from yeast dough and are fluffy.

quiz.q: How long should you steam dumplings?
quiz.explanation: Steaming for 10 minutes cooks the filling and wrapper through.

quiz.q: What is a common substitute for cabbage in dumpling filling in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Spinach or kale are widely available and work well in dumplings.

quiz.q: How do you make potstickers crispy on the bottom?
options: B) Fry then steam, then uncover to crisp
quiz.explanation: Frying then steaming then uncovering gives a crispy bottom and cooked top.

quiz.q: What is a good dipping sauce for dumplings?
options: B) Soy sauce, vinegar, and chili oil
quiz.explanation: This classic mix of soy, vinegar, and chili oil is standard for dumplings.

quiz.q: What are the three core condiments mentioned in the lesson?
options: B) Soy sauce blend, chili oil, hoisin
quiz.explanation: The lesson focuses on soy sauce blend, chili oil, and hoisin sauce.

quiz.q: How do you make chili oil?
options: A) Mix chili flakes with cold oil
B) Pour hot oil over chili flakes and spices
C) Boil chili flakes in water
quiz.explanation: Hot oil poured over chili flakes and aromatics infuses the oil.

quiz.q: What is a key ingredient in hoisin sauce?
quiz.explanation: Peanut butter (or groundnut paste) gives hoisin its sweet, nutty flavor.

quiz.q: How should you store homemade chili oil?
options: B) In a jar in the fridge
quiz.explanation: A sealed jar in the fridge keeps chili oil fresh for months.

quiz.q: What can you use instead of miso in a ramen broth in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Groundnut paste adds a rich, nutty umami similar to miso.

quiz.q: Why is it important to label takeaway containers?
options: B) To identify dish and spice level
quiz.explanation: Labeling helps customers know what they are eating and avoid allergies.

quiz.q: What is a good packaging choice for hot noodle soup?
quiz.explanation: A lined paper box insulates and prevents leaks for soup noodles.

quiz.q: How can you prevent stir-fried noodles from becoming soggy in takeaway?
quiz.explanation: Packing sauce separately keeps noodles from absorbing liquid and getting soggy.

quiz.q: What is a traditional and eco-friendly wrapping for takeaway in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Banana leaves are biodegradable and commonly used for wrapping food.

quiz.q: What is the recommended portion size for a main noodle dish?
quiz.explanation: A main dish portion of 300-400g is satisfying and standard for takeaway.
